blogPosts.title: Designing APIs that feel instant to the frontend
blogPosts.excerpt: A practical checklist for API design that reduces front-end work and speeds delivery.
blogPosts.content:
# Designing APIs that feel instant to the frontend

When the API is predictable, the UI ships faster. This post captures the checklist I use to keep responses consistent, easy to consume, and stable across releases.

## The north star

> The best API response is the one the UI does not have to reshape.

I optimize for three things: **shape stability**, **clear errors**, and **fast iteration**.

## Response shape rules

- Return a top-level `data` object every time.
- Add `meta` only when it truly matters.
- Avoid conditional keys that appear only sometimes.

Example response:

```json
{
  "data": {
    "items": [],
    "next": null
  },
  "meta": {
    "request_id": "a1b2"
  }
}
```

## Error contract

Errors should follow one predictable shape:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "validation_error",
    "message": "Email is required",
    "fields": {
      "email": ["Required"]
    }
  }
}
```

## Pagination that is easy to render

| Field | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `next` | string or null | URL for next page |
| `prev` | string or null | URL for previous page |
| `items` | array | Always present |

## Caching notes

- Use `ETag` for list endpoints.
- Keep ordering stable to avoid UI jitter.
- Return `updated_at` for detail pages.

## Quick checklist

- [x] Stable keys for all responses
- [x] Strict error schema
- [x] Pagination with `next` and `prev`
- [x] ISO 8601 timestamps

## Example request

```bash
curl -H "Accept: application/json" https://api.example.com/v1/projects
```

## Example response

```json
{
  "data": {
    "items": [
      {
        "id": 12,
        "title": "InsightHub Analytics",
        "featured": true,
        "updated_at": "2026-04-12T10:30:00Z"
      }
    ],
    "next": null,
    "prev": null
  }
}
```

If you are starting fresh, copy this structure and you will save front-end time on every feature.

---

**Related:** [API design notes](https://example.com/api-notes)

blogPosts.title: UX writing that reduces support tickets
blogPosts.excerpt: Small changes in copy can reduce confusion and cut support load. Here is a tested approach.
blogPosts.content:
# UX writing that reduces support tickets

Words shape behavior. A single label can add or remove friction from a flow. This post shows a simple framework I use to improve copy and reduce user errors.

## A quick example

Before: **Create**

After: **Create invoice**

The second option removes ambiguity and reduces mistakes.

## The 3-step framework

1. **Name the action**
2. **Clarify the outcome**
3. **Set expectations**

### 1) Name the action

Use verb-first labels that say exactly what will happen.

- Good: `Save draft`
- Bad: `Submit`

### 2) Clarify the outcome

Add a short supporting line below the button:

> You can edit the draft before sending.

### 3) Set expectations

Call out timing and limits in the UI:

```text
This import may take 2-3 minutes.
We will email you when it is ready.
```

## A tiny checklist

- [x] Button text is specific
- [x] One sentence sets expectations
- [x] Error messages explain the fix

## Error messages that help

| Error | Better |
| --- | --- |
| "Invalid" | "Password must be at least 12 characters" |
| "Failed" | "Upload failed. Try a smaller file." |

## A short script for reviews

```js
const auditCopy = (label, helper) => {
  if (!label || label.length < 3) return 'Label too short';
  if (helper && helper.length > 120) return 'Helper too long';
  return 'OK';
};
```

## Final thought

> Clear copy is a feature, not an afterthought.

---

**Further reading:** [Writing for interfaces](https://example.com/ux-writing)

blogPosts.title: Shipping a portfolio in 10 days: a real plan
blogPosts.excerpt: A day-by-day plan with constraints, scope control, and a launch checklist.
blogPosts.content:
# Shipping a portfolio in 10 days: a real plan

This is a realistic plan for a tight timeline. It is not about perfection. It is about shipping a credible product.

## Scope

I cap scope to **5 pages** and **3 sections** each. If a section does not support hiring goals, it ships later.

## Day-by-day

### Day 1: Direction

- Write the project goal
- Pick the stack
- Define the content outline

### Day 2: Layout

- Build the nav and hero
- Set type scale
- Define spacing system

### Day 3: Projects

- Add 3 projects with screenshots
- Write impact-focused descriptions

### Day 4: Blog

- Add 3 posts
- Ensure markdown renders correctly

### Day 5: Contact

- Add a form
- Confirm email delivery

### Day 6-7: Polish

- Fix responsive layout
- Check spacing and rhythm
- Add subtle motion

### Day 8: Perf

- Compress images
- Verify lighthouse scores

### Day 9: QA

- Test on 3 screen sizes
- Fix edge cases

### Day 10: Launch

- Point domain
- Share with 5 peers

## The launch checklist

- [x] No console errors
- [x] Forms validated
- [x] 404 page exists
- [x] Metadata set
- [x] Analytics added

## Example project write-up

```md
**Result:** Increased weekly signups by 28%
**Stack:** React, Django, Postgres
**Work:** Rebuilt onboarding and added dashboard analytics
```

## Image test

![Sample hero](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1498050108023-c5249f4df085?w=1200)

## Final note

I ship with a timer. It keeps the work honest.
